title: Order extras that multiply the classes
hints: If marketing asks for a fourth extra, how many new classes would you have to write, and what would each one repeat from the others?
Let an extra be an order itself: it holds another order, asks it for its price and description, and adds its own charge and text. Then extras can be stacked on anything.

quiz.question: Which principle does this code break most clearly?
quiz.explanation: Every new extra forces new subclasses: GiftWrappedExpressOrder and InsuredExpressOrder exist only because two extras were combined, and each repeats the price and description logic of the single-extra classes. Each new extra means writing a whole new set of classes (the number would double every time) instead of adding one small piece, which is exactly what the Open/Closed principle warns against. It also means one class carries the knowledge of several extras at once, which strains Single Responsibility.

steps.title: Give every order one common type
steps.md:
Right now only `BasicOrder` can be an order, so nothing else can be used in its place.

The starter already has an interface `Order` (file `Order.java`) with two methods: `double price()` and `String description()`.

1. Make `BasicOrder` implement `Order` (`public class BasicOrder implements Order`).
2. Change the parameter of `show` in `Main` from `BasicOrder` to `Order`.

Nothing else changes: the old subclasses still extend `BasicOrder`, so they keep working. Run the tests: `S1:` should pass.

steps.title: Make gift wrapping an order that wraps another order
steps.md:
Fill in the class `GiftWrap` (file `GiftWrap.java`). It already `implements Order` and has the constructor `public GiftWrap(Order inner)`.

1. Store the `Order` that is passed in a `private final Order inner` field.
2. `price()` returns `inner.price() + 3.0`.
3. `description()` returns `inner.description() + " + gift wrap"`.

The constructor takes an `Order`, not a `BasicOrder`: that is what lets `GiftWrap` wrap anything. For example `new GiftWrap(new BasicOrder("Book", 12.0))` has price `15.0` and description `Book + gift wrap`. Run the tests: `S2:` should pass.

steps.title: Add express handling and stack the extras
steps.md:
Fill in the class `ExpressHandling` (file `ExpressHandling.java`) the same way: it `implements Order`, has the constructor `public ExpressHandling(Order inner)`, and keeps the order it wraps in a field.

1. `price()` returns `inner.price() + 7.0`.
2. `description()` returns `inner.description() + " + express"`.

Because both classes are orders that wrap an order, they can be combined in any order and repeated:

- `new ExpressHandling(new GiftWrap(new BasicOrder("Book", 12.0)))` has price `22.0` and description `Book + gift wrap + express`.
- `new GiftWrap(new ExpressHandling(new BasicOrder("Book", 12.0)))` has description `Book + express + gift wrap`.

The description lists the extras in the order they were applied. Run the tests: `S3:` should pass.

steps.title: Prove a new extra needs no change, then delete the combinations
steps.md:
The test file defines its own extra, `Insurance` (+2.5, ` + insurance`), as a class that implements `Order` and wraps an `Order`. It must work stacked with your classes without you changing any of them.

Your job in this step is to finish the refactoring:

1. Change `Main` so it builds its four orders with `BasicOrder`, `GiftWrap` and `ExpressHandling` instead of the combination classes. It must print exactly the four lines from the example.
2. Delete the five classes `GiftWrappedOrder`, `ExpressOrder`, `GiftWrappedExpressOrder`, `InsuredOrder` and `InsuredExpressOrder`. Nothing needs them any more.

Run `Main` to check the output, then run the tests: `S4:` should pass.

roles.name: Decorator
roles.is: the shape GiftWrap and ExpressHandling share: each implements Order and holds an Order to forward to

roles.name: ConcreteDecorator
roles.is: GiftWrap and ExpressHandling (and the Insurance class in the tests)

reveal.summary: Decorator lets you add behaviour to an object by wrapping it in another object with the same interface, so extras stack in any combination instead of needing a subclass for each one. A new extra is one new class and the existing ones stay untouched, which is Open/Closed in action. Do not use it when there are only one or two fixed variations (a plain subclass or a flag is simpler), or when callers need the exact concrete type or when the order of wrapping would be easy to get wrong and hard to debug.
